data.title: META Stock Drops 3.3% After New Mexico Jury Finds that Meta Platforms Misled Facebook Users Over Data Safety Rules
data.description:
Meta Platforms' stock (META) dropped on the news of a legal defeat in Santa Fe. Shares of Meta fell 3.33% to close at $751.66 on Friday as investors reacted to a New Mexico court ruling against the tech giant.

A state jury found that Meta misled Facebook users about its user data rules and content moderation. The trial covered claims stemming from the 2016 Cambridge Analytica scandal, where outside groups gathered data from up to 87 million Facebook users.

Jury Finds that Meta Misled the Public on Data Safety Rules

State lawyers argued that Meta misled Facebook users by promising them control over their personal details while sharing information with outside apps. Jurors agreed that 26 out of 29 statements made by Meta leaders or company blogs were misleading.

Meta spokespeople stated that the firm disagrees with the verdict and plans to appeal. Company leaders maintain that Meta protects user details and retains First Amendment rights to run its social platforms.

Judge Weighs Maximum Fines and Safety Audits for Meta

Judge Francis Mathew will now determine civil fines after jurors found over 43 million total violations. State laws allow fines up to $5,000 per violation, which means total costs could rise quickly if the judge orders maximum penalties.

State officials have also asked the court to force Meta to run independent safety audits on its data rules. This trial marks the second time in six months that a New Mexico jury has ruled against Meta over user safety claims.

Repeat Legal Battles Could Weigh on Meta Stock's Outlook

This New Mexico verdict adds to a long list of legal fights for Meta over platform safety and user privacy.

In March, a Santa Fe jury ordered Meta to pay $375 million over child safety claims, which later grew to $567 million after a second trial phase.

Soon after, Meta agreed to pay up to $17 billion in a multi-state settlement covering youth addiction claims across 47 states. These repeated legal cases threaten Meta's profit margins through rising legal fees and strict court-ordered audits.

While Meta holds strong annual cash flows and a dominant ad business, ongoing court losses create uncertainty for investors. If judges force Meta to change how it uses personal data to show targeted ads, lower ad revenues could push Meta stock down further over the coming quarters.

data.title: McDonald's Commits $8.5 Billion to Help Stores and Boost U.S. Sales with Voice AI Tools and Updated Menu Options
data.description:
McDonald's (MCD) executives have laid out an $8.5 billion support plan through 2036 to help local restaurant owners rebuild stores and speed up food prep. The move came as McDonald's management projected that third-quarter U.S. sales will turn slightly negative following a slow summer.

To help local owners, McDonald's will give direct cash help and rent cuts to offset rising costs for food and equipment. Company bosses expect this support to boost cash flow by about $100,000 a year for the average U.S. location.

McDonald's Adds Drive-Thru AI and Menu Board Ads

As part of its operational plan, McDonald's will bring voice AI tools to drive-thru lanes to help take orders in English and Spanish. The chain has also started running third-party ads on digital menu boards inside stores to bring in extra cash from daily foot traffic.

data.title: Synopsys Stock Gets New Street-High $700 Price Target from HSBC – Here's Why
data.description:
Chip design software company Synopsys (SNPS) received a major upgrade from HSBC (HSBC) on Friday as the bank argued that artificial intelligence could transform how the company makes money. 4.5-star HSBC analyst Frank Lee upgraded Synopsys to Buy from Hold and raised his price target by $210 to a street high of $700 from $490. Lee believes that Synopsys can shift from a slower-growing software business into a faster-growing AI beneficiary as it changes how it sells chip design technology.

That change starts with Synopsys moving away from simply building software once and selling licenses to many customers. Instead, the company is working more closely with semiconductor customers on custom chip designs. That allows Synopsys to collect normal licensing revenue while also earning royalties based on how many chips its customers eventually sell.

Therefore, if a customer produces more chips, Synopsys can make more money without having to sell another traditional software license.

Lee believes that this model could work well with large cloud companies and custom chip makers. Foundries could also use the service. More importantly, he expects the royalty revenue to carry high profit margins, which could help earnings grow much faster.

AI Agents Could Change How Customers Pay Synopsys

The second part of HSBC's thesis comes from agentic AI. Today, engineers typically use Synopsys electronic design automation software to help design chips. Lee expects that AI agents will eventually handle much more of that work themselves. That could change how Synopsys charges customers.

Instead of selling subscriptions mainly for human engineers, the company could move toward a model that combines subscriptions with usage-based charges. Therefore, customers could pay more as AI agents use Synopsys tools more often.

This matters because an AI agent can potentially complete far more design work than one engineer. As a result, greater software usage could create additional revenue for Synopsys.

Lee believes that these two changes could lift earnings significantly and cause investors to value Synopsys more like a high-growth AI company rather than a traditional software provider.

data.title: Rivian Stock May Soon Get a New Catalyst… And It's Not EV Deliveries
data.description:
EV maker Rivian Automotive (RIVN) now has a stock catalyst that isn't vehicle deliveries. Indeed, its autonomy software is starting to look like a product investors could value separately from the vehicles themselves. On September 29, Rivian's autonomy and AI leadership will appear at the Evercore ADAS, AV & AI Forum. The timing is important because Rivian plans to introduce point-to-point assisted driving later this year and is preparing the R2 platform for more advanced autonomy.

The R2 is already in customer hands. Deliveries started on June 9, with the R2 Performance starting at $57,990. Rivian also plans to launch the $44,990 R2 Standard in 2027. That gives investors a clear way to judge whether Rivian can turn software from a useful vehicle feature into a recurring source of value.

Catalysts that May Push the Stock Higher

RivianOS 2 may be one of the most important parts of this story. Rivian moved both the R1 and R2 onto one software platform this month. That should make it easier to roll out updates across the fleet and could support paid features such as Autonomy+. R2 already offers hands-free assisted driving across 3.5 million miles of roads in the U.S. and Canada.

The larger opportunity comes from ride-hailing company Uber Technologies (UBER). Uber agreed to invest up to $1.25 billion in Rivian through 2031 if Rivian reaches certain autonomy milestones. The companies expect an initial fleet of 10,000 autonomous R2 robotaxis, with an option for up to 40,000 more. Initial commercial deployments are planned for 2028.

That partnership matters because it could change how investors look at Rivian. If the company proves that its self-driving technology works at scale, investors may start to value part of Rivian more like a software and technology platform than a traditional automaker.

There is also financial evidence that supports this idea. Rivian's software and services revenue reached $515 million in the second quarter, with a 42% gross margin. Total gross profit reached $179 million. Those figures help explain why software could play an important role in Rivian's path toward stronger financials.

Risks to Watch Out For

The main risk is that Rivian still has a lot to prove. Its autonomy technology needs more technical validation and regulatory approval. Uber's additional investment also depends on Rivian meeting specific milestones.

At the same time, the R2 production ramp could put pressure on costs. Rivian still expects a full-year adjusted EBITDA loss of $1.8 billion to $2.0 billion. Adjusted EBITDA is a common measure of operating performance that excludes some expenses. Simply put, Rivian is still losing a large amount of money from its operations, so its software progress will eventually need to help reduce cash use.

There is also a timing issue with the lower-priced R2. The $44,990 R2 Standard is not expected until 2027. Until then, Rivian must show that its higher-priced R2 versions can attract enough demand while the company continues to improve manufacturing costs.

data.title: Bill Ackman Asks If the AI Boom Is Breaking the Fed's Inflation Playbook
data.description:
Billionaire investor Bill Ackman is questioning whether Federal Reserve rate hikes still reduce inflation the way policymakers expect, as AI and energy investment stays strong. "What if higher rates don't reduce demand and investment because the demand for intelligence and energy is unaffected by higher rates?" the Pershing Square (PS) CEO asked. Ackman argues that companies could keep spending heavily on AI infrastructure even when borrowing gets more expensive because the potential financial rewards are so large.

Normally, the Fed raises short-term interest rates because higher borrowing costs are expected to reduce spending and investment. That lower demand can then reduce pressure on prices.

Ackman questions whether that process works as well when technology companies feel that they must keep spending on computing power to compete in AI. Energy demand connected to data infrastructure could also stay strong for the same reason. Therefore, companies may continue to invest even after rates rise.

Ackman also argues that higher rates can create another problem because businesses face larger interest expenses. Those costs can eventually get passed through the economy through higher prices. That led Ackman to question whether additional rate hikes could actually add to inflation instead of reducing it.

Critics Say Recent History Supports Higher Rates

Other investors and economists pushed back strongly against Ackman's argument. Discipline Funds founder Cullen Roche pointed to what happened after U.S. inflation reached roughly 9% in 2022. The Fed raised rates above 5%, and inflation subsequently fell to about 3%.

Roche also pointed to Turkey, where policymakers cut rates while inflation eventually climbed to above 80%. He argued that those examples contradict the idea that higher interest rates generally cause more inflation.

However, Ben Borter of Slack Water Capital supported part of Ackman's argument. He said that much of today's inflation comes from limited supply rather than excessive demand. Under that view, higher borrowing costs can discourage companies from adding new supply. That could make shortages worse and put additional pressure on prices.

data.title: U.S. Investigation into CrowdStrike (CRWD) Ends with No Charges Being Filed
data.description:
U.S. prosecutors have ended an investigation into CrowdStrike Holdings (CRWD) without pursuing any charges against the cybersecurity firm. Federal prosecutors and regulators had been examining CrowdStrike's handling of transactions since early 2025, including executive knowledge of deals the company was engaged in.

However, the U.S. Justice Department says it has now finished its review of CrowdStrike and will not be pursuing any criminal or civil actions against the firm. Prosecutors from the Manhattan U.S. attorney's office did not provide any explanations concerning their findings or reasons for closing the investigation. The Austin, Texas-based company stated in August that it was cooperating with a Justice Department investigation regarding its accounting and "transactions with certain customers."

The end of the Justice Department investigation removes a cloud that had been hanging over CrowdStrike in recent months.

Providing AI Security

CrowdStrike is best-known for Falcon, its cloud-based cybersecurity platform that helps companies protect endpoints, cloud workloads, identities, and other critical parts of their technology infrastructure. The platform could become increasingly important as businesses deploy artificial intelligence (AI) tools and autonomous agents.

The problems that could be caused by AI technologies are seen as a big opportunity for CrowdStrike and other cybersecurity firms. Analysts say that potential problems caused by the technologies won't disappear if the development of AI systems slows. After all, many companies already use AI, cloud computing, and automated systems throughout their operations.

The Rally in Cybersecurity Stocks

Owing to AI demand, CRWD stock has gained 117% this year, more than doubling. Other cybersecurity stocks have risen as much or more. The rapid gains have made security stocks some of the most expensive in the market. CrowdStrike's stock is now priced at more than 170 times estimated earnings, which is second only to Tesla (TSLA).

The rally is in stark contrast to the beginning of the year, when AI disruption fears sparked a major selloff across the software industry. While those worries have subsided for many software companies, including cybersecurity firms, a series of recent warnings from within the AI industry about grave threats posed by the technology have provided investors with another reason to buy CRWD stock.
